deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler treats a wooden column as a body that resists bending, with flexural rigidity ('moment de roideur') Ekk; in modern terms Ekk is EI. To measure Ekk he clamps the column at its base AB and pushes its top sideways with a horizontal force F. On the previous page he gives the small-deflection result Dδ = F·AC³/(3Ekk), i.e. the modern cantilever formula δ = FL³/(3EI). He also quotes a corrected form, Ekk = F·AC²(AC/(3Dδ) − 1/2).

§IV (end): Ekk depends only on the cross-section and the material, not on the length or the load. So the tip deflection Dδ must scale as follows:
- with the force fixed, Dδ is proportional to AC³;
- with the length fixed, Dδ is proportional to F;
- in general, Dδ is proportional to F·AC³.
Repeating the test with different lengths and loads therefore gives redundant measurements of the single constant Ekk, which is a consistency check on the model.

§V: Euler asks how Ekk depends on the cross-section.
- For a rectangular prism he separates the 'épaisseur' AB, in the plane of bending, from the 'largeur' Aa, perpendicular to it.
- He calls it 'assez évident' that Ekk is proportional to the width.
- Because the thickness resists bending more, he suggests Ekk goes as its square ('raison doublée') or even its cube ('triplée').
- Hence for a circular cylinder Ekk would go as d³, 'or perhaps rather' d⁴ ('quarré quarré du diametre').
In modern terms I = bh³/12 for the rectangle and πd⁴/64 for the circle. So the linear width law, the cubic thickness option and the d⁴ option are all correct, and they are mutually consistent (h³ × width ~ d⁴).

§VI: Euler proposes a programme:
- experiments on many cross-sectional shapes, bent in different directions (the anisotropy of bending stiffness about different axes);
- experiments on different materials;
- eventually a theory giving a rule for Ekk from material and cross-section.
The next page adds that this would extend to columns of variable thickness, Ekk(x).

The purpose of all this is to supply the constant needed in his buckling formula for columns.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The scaling Dδ ∝ F·AC³ is exact within linear small-deflection theory.
The cross-section dependence is only conjectured, with hedging (square or cube; d³ or d⁴). The correct cube and fourth-power laws are stated as possibilities, not derived.
The correction term −1/2 in the formula quoted on the previous page has no counterpart in the linear theory. That issue belongs to the earlier page, not this one.

ideas.what: Scaling of cantilever tip deflection with load and length (δ ∝ FL³), used as a consistency test for measuring the bending stiffness
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I De curvis elasticis (1744), §39 as cited; E238

ideas.what: Flexural rigidity linear in width and cubic (or quadratic) in thickness; for circular section proportional to d⁴ (or d³)
ideas.modern_name: Second moment of area, I = bh³/12, πd⁴/64
ideas.usually_credited_to: Correct derivation usually credited to later workers (Coulomb 1776, Navier 1820s); Euler's conjecture discussed by Truesdell 1960
ideas.where_published: E238 (this memoir); discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Programme to separate the material and cross-section contributions to Ekk, including bending in different directions and variable cross-section
ideas.modern_name: EI = modulus × geometric moment; principal axes of bending; tapered columns
ideas.where_published: E238; Euler's later column papers (e.g. on columns of variable thickness, 1778)

deep.surprise_reason: Euler's hedged guess that stiffness goes as width × thickness² or thickness³, with d⁴ for cylinders, is a nice anticipation of I ∝ bh³. However, it is known and discussed by Truesdell in the Opera omnia historical commentary, so it is not missing from the record.
